p.seg: I am a descendant of Emperor Gāoyáng,
my late father was called Bóyōng.
When the Shetí star pointed to the first month,
on the Gēngyín day I was born.
My father, observing my natal aspect,
bestowed on me an auspicious name.
He named me Zhèngzé,
and styled me Língjūn.
I possess such abundant inner virtues,
and add to them outward talents.
I clad myself with riverside angelica,
and thread autumn orchids as pendants.
Swiftly I flow as if racing against time,
fearing years will not wait for me.
At dawn I pluck magnolias on the hill,
at dusk gather evergreen herbs in isles.
Sun and moon swiftly pass without lingering,
spring and autumn alternate in succession.
Seeing plants and trees wither and fall,
I fear the beauty's fading years.
Not holding to vigor while discarding filth,
why not change this way?
Mounting fine steeds to gallop forth,
come, I'll lead the way ahead!
The ancient three kings were pure and perfect,
where fragrant flowers truly gathered.
Mingled with pepper and cassia,
why only thread orchids and angelicas?
Yáo and Shùn were bright and upright,
following the right path they found the way.
Why were Jié and Zhòu so reckless,
taking shortcuts to stumble?
The factionists seek only pleasure,
their path dark and perilous.
Do I fear calamity for myself?
I dread the royal chariot's ruin.
Hastening to serve before and after,
to follow the footsteps of former kings.
The prince ignores my loyal heart,
instead believes slander and rages.
I know frankness brings trouble,
yet endure and cannot desist.
I call Heaven to witness,
all for the sake of the Divine One.
He pledged to meet at dusk,
yet midway changed his course.
First he made covenant with me,
later regretted and turned elsewhere.
I do not mind the parting,
but grieve his constant changes.
I've cultivated orchids over nine fields,
and planted huì flowers on hundred acres.
Plots of liúyí and jiēchē,
mixed with dùhéng and fragrant zhǐ.
Hoping their branches grow lush and tall,
I await the time to harvest.
Though they wither, what harm is there?
I mourn all fragrances turning to weeds.
All compete in greed and advancement,
insatiable in their demands.
Forgiving themselves while judging others,
each harbors jealousy in heart.
Rushing wildly in pursuit,
is not what my heart seeks.
Old age gradually approaches,
fearing my good name unestablished.
At dawn I drink magnolia's falling dew,
at dusk feed on autumn chrysanthemum petals.
If my feelings are truly beautiful and essential,
why grieve over long hunger?
Gathering roots to tie angelicas,
threading falling stamens of ivy.
Straightening cassia to thread huì flowers,
twisting húshéng vines into cords.
I emulate the ancient sages,
not what the vulgar world wears.
Though out of step with modern men,
I wish to follow Péngxián's legacy.
Heaving long sighs, wiping tears,
grieving life's many hardships.
Though I love beauty and restrain myself,
morning reproached, evening dismissed.
Dismissed for wearing huì sachets,
and again for gathering angelicas.
If it's what my heart deems good,
even nine deaths I'll not regret.
Resenting the prince's waywardness,
he never understands people's hearts.
Many women envy my fine brows,
slandering me as licentious.
Truly the times favor cunning,
disregarding rules to change measures.
Rejecting straight lines to chase curves,
competing in flattery as the norm.
Depressed and troubled, I stand alone,
alone in distress at this time.
Rather die suddenly and vanish,
than bear such demeanor.
Fierce birds do not flock together,
since ancient times it's been so.
How can square and circle fit?
Different paths never find peace.
Subduing heart and restraining will,
enduring blame and bearing insults.
Embracing purity to die upright,
is what former sages esteemed.
Regretting I misjudged the road,
pausing long, I'll turn back.
Turning my chariot to retrace the path,
before going too far astray.
Walking my horse through orchid shores,
galloping up pepper hills to rest.
Advancing brings blame and rejection,
retreating to mend my former dress.
Making lotus leaves into a coat,
gathering lotus petals for a skirt.
If none know me, so be it,
as long as my feelings stay fragrant.
Raising my hat high and towering,
lengthening my pendant, dazzling.
Fragrance and luster blend together,
only my bright essence remains undimmed.
Suddenly looking back, gazing afar,
I'll go observe the four wilds.
Adorned with lavish, colorful pendants,
their fragrance grows ever stronger.
People each have their own joys,
I alone love beauty as constant.
Even dismembered, I'd not change,
how could my heart be punished?
Nǚ Xū, tender with concern,
repeatedly chides me, saying:
"Gǔn, too stubborn, lost his life,
finally dying in Yǔ's wilderness.
Why so outspoken and fond of beauty,
alone possessing such fine virtues?
Weeds fill the rooms,
yet you stand apart, refusing to wear them.
You can't explain to everyone door-to-door,
who will understand our true feelings?
The world flocks together and loves cliques,
why so solitary and not listening to me?"
Following ancient sages to guide my heart,
sighing with frustration, I endure this.
Crossing Yuán and Xiāng, heading south,
to address Chónghuà with my plea:
"Qǐ brought down the Jiǔbiàn and Jiǔgē,
Xià indulged in pleasure and excess.
Not planning for difficulties ahead,
five sons thus lost their home.
Yì roamed excessively in hunting,
loved shooting great foxes.
Such disorder rarely ends well,
Zhuó coveted and took his household.
Ào, clad in brute strength,
indulged desires without restraint.
Daily reveling, forgetting himself,
his head thus fell and rolled.
Jié of Xià constantly transgressed,
thus met with disaster.
Zhòu of Yīn minced his victims,
so Yīn's lineage did not last long.
Tāng and Yǔ were solemn and reverent,
Zhōu discussed the Way without error.
Promoting the worthy, employing the able,
following rules without deviation.
August Heaven shows no partiality,
observing virtue to assist accordingly.
Only the sage kings with splendid deeds,
may rule over this land below.
Looking back and gazing forward,
observing people's ultimate aims.
Which unrighteousness can be employed?
Which goodness can be followed?
Though I risk death at the brink,
looking back, I have no regret.
Not measuring the socket before setting the tenon,
was why former sages were minced.
Sobbing endlessly, I'm filled with sorrow,
grieving I was born at the wrong time.
Gathering soft orchids to wipe tears,
soaking my lapel with streaming drops."
Kneeling, spreading my gown to plead,
clearly I've found this central truth;
Harnessing jade dragons, riding phoenixes,
I soar on dusty winds.
At dawn I start from Cāngwú,
by evening reach Xuánpǔ;
Wishing to linger at divine gates,
the sun swiftly nears dusk.
I order Xīhé to slow the pace,
The road stretches endlessly far,
I'll search above and below.
I water my steed at the Xiánchí pool,
And tie its reins to the Fúsāng tree.
Breaking a Ruòmù branch to brush the sun,
I wander freely and take my ease.
I send Wàngshū ahead as my forerunner,
And Fēilián to follow in swift pursuit.
The Luán and Huáng birds herald my approach,
But the Thunder God says all is not ready.
I command the Phoenix to soar upward,
Continuing day and night without rest.
The whirlwind gathers and draws apart,
Leading clouds and rainbows to welcome me.
In chaotic swirls they part and unite,
Shimmering and shifting up and down.
I bid the Heavenly Gatekeeper open the gate,
But he leans against the Chānghé and stares at me.
As daylight fades and the day wears on,
I knot orchids and linger in waiting.
The world is murky and indiscriminate,
Hiding beauty and fostering envy.
At dawn I shall cross the Báishuǐ River,
And on Lángfēng Mountain tie my horse.
Suddenly I look back and shed tears,
Grieving that this high peak has no maiden.
Hastily I wander to the Spring Palace,
Plucking jade branches to adorn my girdle.
Before their radiant blossoms fade,
I shall seek a maiden below to gift them.
I command Fēnglóng to ride the clouds,
To find where Fúfēi dwells.
I untie my girdle to pledge my words,
And send Jiǎnxiū as my envoy.
In chaotic swirls they part and unite,
Suddenly wayward and hard to sway.
At dusk she returns to Qióngshí to rest,
At dawn she washes her hair in Wěipán.
Proud she guards her beauty,
Daily indulging in pleasure and idle roam.
Though truly fair, she lacks propriety,
So I turn away and seek another.
Gazing afar to the four extremes,
I roam the heavens and then descend.
Beholding the lofty Yáotái Tower,
I see the lovely daughter of Yǒusōng.
I bid the Zhèn bird be my matchmaker,
But it tells me she is not good.
The male dove chirps and flies off,
But I dislike its frivolous cunning.
My heart hesitates and doubts,
Wishing to go myself, yet I cannot.
The Phoenix has already brought the gift,
I fear Gāoxīn may precede me.
Wishing to go far, yet having no place to stay,
I wander aimlessly and take my ease.
Before Shàokāng had wed,
The two Yáo sisters of Yǒuyú remained.
My envoy is weak, my matchmaker clumsy,
Fearing their words lack firmness.
The world is murky and envious of worth,
Hiding beauty and praising evil.
The inner chambers are deep and remote,
The wise king remains unawakened.
Holding my feelings unreleased,
How can I endure this eternally?
I gather Qióngmáo and bamboo slips,
Commanding Língfēn to divine for me.
He says, "When two beauties meet, they unite,
But who is truly virtuous and worthy of longing?"
Thinking of the vastness of the nine regions,
Is it only here that maidens dwell?
He urges, "Go far without doubt,
Who seeking beauty would reject you?
Where is there no fragrant grass?
Why cling to your old homeland?"
The world is dark and dazzling,
Who can discern my good and evil?
People's likes and dislikes differ,
Only these partisans are uniquely strange.
They wear mugwort stuffed at their waists,
Saying orchids are not fit to wear.
They cannot even judge plants rightly,
How can they assess true jade's beauty?
They stuff their sachets with dung and soil,
Claiming Shēnjiāo peppers are not fragrant.
Wishing to follow Língfēn's auspicious divination,
My heart hesitates and doubts.
Wūxián will descend at dusk,
I bring pepper and rice to welcome him.
A hundred spirits shade the sky as they descend,
The Jiǔyí peaks brightly greet them.
Radiantly they display their divine power,
Telling me auspicious tales of old.
They urge, "Rise and fall, go up and down,
Seek those who share your measure.
Tāng and Yǔ strictly sought harmony,
With Zhì and Gāoyáo they found accord.
If your inner self is truly virtuous,
Why need a matchmaker's aid?
Fù Yuè labored with a mortar at Fùyán,
Wǔdīng employed him without doubt.
Lǚ Wàng once wielded a butcher's knife,
He met King Wén of Zhōu and was raised.
Nìng Qì sang his songs,
Duke Huán of Qí heard and made him minister.
While your years are not yet late,
And time is still abundant.
Fear the cuckoo's early cry,
Making all flowers lose their fragrance."
How my jade pendant stands tall,
Yet the crowd obscures it darkly.
These partisans are untrustworthy,
Fearing envy, they would break it.
The times are chaotic and changing,
How can I linger here?
Orchids and zhǐ flowers turn scentless,
Quán and huì become mere weeds.
Why have yesterday's fragrant plants,
Today turned to this vile mugwort?
Is there any other reason,
Than the harm of neglecting self-cultivation?
I thought the orchid could be relied on,
But it proved hollow and showy.
Forsaking its beauty to follow the crowd,
It barely ranks among the fragrant.
The pepper is flattering and arrogant,
The shā fruit seeks to fill the sachet.
Striving only for advancement,
How can any fragrance be revered?
Since the world flows with the current,
Who can avoid changing?
Seeing pepper and orchid thus,
How much more jiēchē and jiānglí herbs?
Only this girdle is truly precious,
Its beauty neglected till now.
Its fragrance rich and hardly faded,
Its scent endures undiminished.
Harmonizing my steps to amuse myself,
I wander freely seeking a maiden.
While my adornments are still splendid,
I shall roam and observe all around.
Since Língfēn gave me an auspicious sign,
I choose a lucky day to depart.
I break jade branches for fine food,
Refine jade dust for provisions.
Harness flying dragons for my chariot,
Adorn it with jade and ivory.
How can hearts at odds unite?
I shall go far and keep my distance.
I turn my path to the Kūnlún Mountains,
A long, winding road ahead.
Raising cloud-banners that dim the sky,
Jade bells chime with a gentle ring.
At dawn I start from the Tiānjīn River,
By evening I reach the western edge.
Phoenixes spread wings bearing my banners,
Soaring high in graceful flight.
Suddenly I tread the Liúshā desert,
Follow the Chìshuǐ River at leisure.
I command蛟龍 to bridge the ford,
Bid the Western God to ferry me across.
The road is long and fraught with hardship,
I order all chariots to wait on paths.
Passing Bùzhōu, I turn left,
Setting the Western Sea as our goal.
Gathering my chariots, a thousand strong,
With jade hubs aligned, we gallop forth.
Driving eight dragons in winding motion,
Cloud banners flutter and sway.
Restraining my will and slowing pace,
My spirit soars high and far.
Playing the "Nine Songs" and dancing to "Sháo",
I take this time to steal some joy.
Ascending to the radiant splendor of heaven,
Suddenly I glance down at my old home.
My driver grieves, my steed longs,
Curling back, it refuses to proceed.
Epilogue:
Let it be enough!
In a land without understanding, none know me,
Why cling to the capital?
Since none are fit to share in virtuous rule,
I shall follow Péngxián to his abode.
2.1 Dōnghuáng Tàiyī
On this auspicious day, a fine hour,
Reverently we please the Supreme Emperor.
Grasping long swords with jade hilts,
They clink and chime, these precious stones.
Jasper mats with jade weights,
Holding clusters of jade flowers.
Huì offerings steamed on orchid mats,
Libations of cassia wine and pepper brew.
Raising drumsticks to beat the drums,
With leisurely beats and solemn songs,
Reeds and zithers join in mighty chorus.
The divine one, majestic in splendid attire,
Fills the hall with pervasive fragrance.
The five tones mingle in rich harmony;
Our lord delights, joyous and well-content.
2.2 The Lord of the Clouds
Bathing in orchid-scented broth, anointed with fragrant herbs,
In rainbow-colored garments like blooming flowers.
The divine one, coiling and lingering, has tarried;
Radiant and brilliant, his splendor knows no end.
He will repose in the Palace of Longevity,
Shining with the same brilliance as the sun and moon.
Dragon-drawn chariot, robes of divinity,
He roams and soars, circling at will.
The glorious spirit, having descended,
Swiftly ascends again amid the clouds.
Gazing beyond Jìzhōu and farther still,
Traversing the four seas, boundless and endless.
Longing for my lord, I sigh deeply,
My heart anxious and troubled with care.
2.3 The Goddess of the Xiāng River
You hesitate and do not come, lingering;
For whom do you wait in the midstream isle?
Lovely and exquisitely adorned,
I speed my cassia boat to meet you.
Let the Yuán and Xiāng rivers still their waves,
And the great river flow calm and smooth!
I watch for you, but you do not come;
Playing my panpipes, for whom do I yearn?
Driving flying dragons, I journey north,
Turning my course toward Dòngtíng Lake.
With fig-leaf curtains and angelica girdings,
Orchid-banner poles and basil oars.
Gazing toward Cényáng's distant shore,
I cross the great river, displaying my spirit.
My spirit-display remains unfulfilled;
The maidens sigh deeply on my behalf.
My tears flow in endless streams;
Secretly longing for you, my heart aches.
Cassia oars and magnolia sweeps,
Cutting through ice and piled snow.
Plucking figs from the water's depth,
Gathering lotus blooms from treetops.
Hearts at odds, the matchmaker's labor is vain;
Love not deep, parting comes lightly.
The rocky shallows rush swiftly by;
The flying dragon glides gracefully.
Faithless friendship breeds lasting sorrow;
Broken promises, claiming no leisure!
At dawn I gallop by the river's edge;
At dusk I rest my steeds on northern isles.
Birds roost upon the rooftops;
Waters encircle the hall below.
I cast my jade ring into the river,
Leave my pendant by the Lǐ River's shore.
Gathering sweet herbs on the isle,
To give as gifts to the maidens below.
Time once gone cannot be regained;
I wander freely, taking my ease.
2.4 The Lady of the Xiāng River
The princess descends on the northern shore;
Gazing afar, my heart fills with sorrow.
Gently blows the autumn breeze;
Dòngtíng's waves stir, leaves fall from trees.
Over white clover I gaze afar,
Preparing for our evening tryst.
Why do birds gather amid duckweeds?
Why are nets hung upon the trees?
The Yuán has its orchids, the Lǐ its angelicas;
Longing for my lord, I dare not speak.
Vaguely, I gaze into the distance,
Watching the flowing waters ripple on.
Why does the elk feed in the courtyard?
Why does the dragon linger in shallow waters?
At dawn I race my horse by the river;
At dusk I cross the western shore.
Hearing my beloved call to me,
I shall hasten to journey with her.
We build our house amid the waters,
Thatched with lotus leaves for a roof.
Walls of basil, courtyard of purple shells,
Hall paved with fragrant pepper.
Beams of cassia, rafters of magnolia,
Lintels of lily magnolia, chamber of peonies.
Weaving fig vines into curtains,
Parting angelica mats, all spread out.
White jade as weights for the mats,
Stone orchids strewn for fragrance.
Lotus rooms thatched with angelica,
Wreathed round with asarums.
A hundred herbs fill the courtyard,
Fragrant blooms adorn porch and gate.
The spirits of Jiǔyí Mountain come in throngs to greet us,
Descending like clouds in multitude.
I cast my sleeve into the river,
Leave my inner robe by the Lǐ River's shore.
Plucking sweet herbs on the river isle,
To give as gifts to one far away.
Time's moments cannot often be seized;
I wander freely, taking my ease.
2.5 The Great Master of Fate
Wide open are the gates of heaven;
I ride forth on dark clouds in throngs.
Commanding the whirlwinds to go before me,
Ordering the rainstorms to cleanse the dust.
You soar and circle, descending;
I cross over Kōngsāng to follow you.
Dense and teeming are the nine realms;
Life and death—all rest in my hands!
Flying high, soaring in tranquility,
Riding pure ether, mastering yīn and yáng.
I journey with you, swift and reverent,
Guiding the Lord to the nine mounds.
Spirit-garments flowing loosely,
Jade pendants glimmering brightly.
Now in shadow, now in light,
None know what I do.
Plucking the sparse hemp's jade-like blooms,
To give to those who dwell apart.
Old age draws gradually near;
Not drawing closer, we grow more distant.
Riding dragons, rumbling onward,
Soaring high, piercing the heavens.
Twining cassia boughs, I wait long;
The more I ponder, the more sorrowful I grow.
What can I do with this sorrow?
I wish that now, as ever, I remain blameless.
For human fate has its appointed course;
Who can control partings and meetings?
2.6 The Lesser Master of Fate
Autumn orchids and meadow-sweet,
Clustering thick below the hall.
Green leaves on pale stems,
Fragrance wafting over me.
All have their own fair children;
Why then, O Sūn, should you grieve?
Autumn orchids, lush and verdant,
Green leaves on purple stems.
The hall is filled with lovely maidens,
But suddenly you glance at me alone.
Entering without word, leaving without farewell,
Riding the whirlwind, bearing cloud-banners.
No sorrow equals parting in life;
No joy equals the joy of new love.
Lotus robes and angelica girdle,
Swiftly you come, suddenly you vanish.
At dusk you lodge at heaven's edge;
Whom do you await at the clouds' border?
I would roam with you to the Nine Rivers,
Where whirlwinds rise and waves surge high.
I would bathe with you in Xiánchí Pool,
Dry your hair on the sunlit slopes.
I watch for my love, but she does not come;
Facing the wind, I sing in despair.
Peacock canopy and kingfisher banners,
You climb the nine heavens, grasping the comet.
Gripping your long sword, protecting the young,
You alone, O Sūn, are fit to rule the people.
2.7 The Lord of the East
The radiant sun rises in the east,
Shining on my railings from the Fúsāng tree.
Patting my horse, I drive at ease;
The night brightens into dawn.
Driving a dragon-chariot, mounted on thunder,
Bearing cloud-banners, curling and streaming.
Sighing deeply, I begin to ascend;
My heart wavers, looking back with longing.
For the sights and sounds delight the people;
The onlookers linger, forgetting to return.
Taut strings and beating drums,
Bells ringing from jade stands,
Flutes and reed-organs playing;
I think of the spirit-priestess, virtuous and fair.
Lightly soaring like kingfishers in flight,
We chant our poems and dance together.
Following the pitch-pipes, keeping the rhythm,
The spirits descend, shading the sun.
In robes of cloud, skirt of rainbow,
I raise my long arrow to shoot the Celestial Wolf.
Grasping my bow, I sink into the west;
Ladling from the Northern Dipper, I drink cassia wine.
Seizing my reins, I soar high and far,
Through the dark and obscure, journeying eastward.
2.8 The River Earl
I roam with you to the Nine Rivers,
Where whirlwinds rise and waves surge high.
Riding a water-chariot with lotus canopy,
Driving twin dragons, flanked by hornless serpents.
Climbing the Kūnlún Mountains, I gaze afar;
My heart soars, boundless and free.
As dusk falls, I linger, forgetting return;
Only at the distant shore do I wake to longing.
With fish-scale roofs and dragon-decked hall,
Purple-shell gate towers and pearl palace walls,
Why does the god dive into water and fall?
Riding white turtles, he chases rainbow fish in throng.
With you I roam the river's isles, my dear,
But broken ice comes floating down, I fear.
You go eastward, hand in hand with me;
I see you off on southern shore, my beauty.
The billows surge up high to greet you nigh;
In long, long lines the fishes for me sigh.
2.9 The Mountain Spirit
It seems there is a lady in the mountain deep,
Clad in creeping vine with belt of wistaria.
With a charming look and a becoming smile,
"Do you love me, my dear? For my form fine?"
Red panthers run before her car
Followed by striped civets on the way;
Her car is built of magnolia,
With banners of cassia boughs, they say.
She is clad in orchids with girdle of azalea.
She gathers wild flowers for her lover far away.
"I live in bamboo grove where I see not the sky,
The way to me is dangerous and hard, so I come late.
I stand alone on mountain top, clouds lie under my feet high;
All is dark and dim below in daytime as at night.
The east wind blows and god sends down rain silently;
I forget to go back in my delight.
When will you come to me, my dear, from the blue sky?
I would pluck the herbs of grace for you in the hill.
Amid the piled-up rocks with creeping vine o'ergrown,
I'm grieved you don't come, my dear, and forget to go home.
Do you remember me, my dear? You have no time, I own.
The lady in the hills is fragrant as the clover,
She drinks from fountain and sleeps 'neath pine and cedar trees.
"Do you remember me, my dear? I am dubious of your love."
The thunder rumbles and the rain darkens the sky;
The monkeys mourn and whine all the night long.
The wind whistles and trees sigh;
I think of you, my dear, in vain with sorrow strong.
2.10 For the Fallen
Gripping our spears, clad in rhinoceros hide,
Chariots clash, daggers gash, side by side.
Flags darken the sun; foes come like clouds in the sky;
Arrows cross and fall; warriors forward vie.
Our line is broken through; our ranks are overrun;
The left horse is dead, the right one wounded sore.
Two wheels are buried; four steeds are held down;
Jade drumsticks beat the drum and urge warriors on.
The heaven falls; gods are angry with everyone;
All are killed and left on the battle ground.
They went out, never to come in;
They're lost on plains and will not be found.
Long swords at waist, bows in hand, head from body torn,
Their hearts are still fearless, though they're forlorn.
Truly brave and also martial,
They were so strong, e'en gods could not hurt them all.
They have died, but their spirit is deathless;
Their souls are hardy, though among the dead peerless.
2.11 Hymn to the Fallen
The rites performed, the drums beat all the way;
The dancers pass lotus from hand to hand;
The fair maid sings slowly and sinks in a trance.
Spring orchid! Autumn chrysanthemum!
Oh, may the rite forever stand!
I ask:
Who could tell the beginning of the past
And hand the story down so long, so fast?
Before heaven and earth were formed,
On what could men make an inquiry informed?
When light and darkness were undivided, still,
Who could see the unseen and know the unknown till
The universe was formed without a form?
How could men know the unshaped from the norm?
How did light come from darkness and divide?
How did the male and female in one coincide?
How were the nine heavens laid out layer on layer?
Who had the measurement and made them fair?
Who did such a deed magnificent?
Who set the heaven in its firmament?
Where is the axis of the sky tied on?
Where are the steelyards of the heaven hung?
Where do eight pillars prop the sky up high?
Why is the earth lower in southeast? Why?
Where do the nine heavens meet in the sky?
How many corners has the earth and the heaven on high?
How many bends and turns have they from east to west?
Who knows their number manifest?
Where does the sky meet with the earth?
How are the twelve zodiac signs set since their birth?
How are the sun and the moon fixed in the sky?
How are the stars arranged on high?
The sun comes up from the Vale of Morning Sun;
It goes down to the Mere when day is done.
From dawn to dusk how many miles has it run?
What virtue has the moon, a waxing and waning one?
What is the advantage to keep a hare in the belly?
The goddess had no husband, why
Had she nine children begot on high?
Where does the gale dwell in the daytime?
Where does the breeze stay at night time?
What door is closed when it is dark?
What door is open at daylight's spark?
When the Horn is not bright, where does the sun hide its ray?
If Gǔn could not stem the flood, I pray,
Why did the people recommend him to do the task?
They all said: "What's the use to ask?
Why not try him and let him do what he could?"
The owl and turtle helped him with mud;
Why did Gǔn follow their advice?
As he was about to succeed in controlling the flood,
Why did the Lord punish him for good?
Kept long on the Feather Mountain, why
For three years was his body left there to lie?
Was Yǔ born from his father's dead body?
How could he succeed his father's work and win such glory?
He carried on the work left undone by his sire;
Thus he accomplished what was his father's desire.
Why did he succeed in continuing his father's task
Though his way was different from what people would ask?
How did he stop the flood surging up to the sky?
How did he pile up the earth so high?
What did the winged dragon mark with its tail on the ground?
Where did the rivers guided by Yǔ abound?
What did his father do in his attempt?
What was accomplished by Yǔ with contempt?
Why was the angry Gong-Hui confined?
Why did the earth tilt down southeast, unkind?
How were the nine regions of the earth laid out?
How were the valleys and rivers dug about?
The rivers flow eastward, but the sea's not filled. Who knows why?
Who knows from east to west which is longer, please reply?
Which is longer from south to north, may I know?
Which is broader and which is narrower also?
Where's the Kunlun Mountain with Hanging Garden?
Where are the nine-fold walls, may I beg your pardon?
Where are the gates opening to the four ways?
Who goes in and out through them all his days?
When the northwestern gate's open, I'm told,
What wind comes through it from the world cold?
Where can't the sun arrive with its light?
How can the Torch Dragon make it bright?
Before the Sun's Charioteer starts to fly,
How can the Flower of Dawn shine in the sky?
Where is the land in winter warm?
Where is the place in summer cool?
Where can be found a forest of stone?
What beast is able to make a speech known?
Where's the hornless dragon, may I be told,
Which bears a yellow bear on its back for a stroll?
Where is the snake with nine heads, swift as a flash?
Where is the land where people never die?
Where are the giants, may I ask you why?
Where grows the magic hemp with nine blooms?
Where is the lifelike snake as huge as mounds?
Where is the Black River and the Dark Hill?
Where's the Mountain of Peril, pray tell?
The people living there never die.
How long does their life last? Reply!
Where is the man-fish big as a whale?
Where is the monstrous bird, pray tell?
How could Yi shoot the suns down from on high?
How could the ravens shed their feather and die?
Great Yǔ devoted all his efforts to his task;
He came down to survey the land, I ask,
How did he meet the maid of Tú Mountain,
And make love with her in a path forsaken?
He married a wife so that he might
Have a son to succeed him and to reign.
Why did he like what others did not
And seek the momentary pleasure he forgot?
Qǐ replaced Yì as lord by and by;
At last he met with calamity.
Why did Qǐ suffer from his enemy
And escape from captivity?
Yì's followers shot at Qǐ without injury.
Why could Yì be replaced and Yǔ's son rule the land?
Why did Qǐ offer sacrifice
And get from Heaven Nine Songs and Nine Ballads nice?
Why did the mother die when her son was born?
Why was her body torn?
The Lord sent down Yí Yì,
To relieve the woes of the Xià people.
Why did he shoot the Hé Bó,
And take Luò Pín as his wife?
With a bow adorned and a swift release,
He shot the great boar.
Why did he offer the fat of steamed meat,
Yet the Lord on High was not pleased?
Zhuó married Chún Hú,
And with his bewitching wife, they plotted.
How could Yì, who pierced through leather,
Be devoured and destroyed by their schemes?
Blocked and desperate, he journeyed west,
How did he cross the rugged cliffs?
Transformed into a yellow bear,
How did the shamans revive him?
All sowed black millet,
And cleared the reeds and rushes.
Why was Gǔn cast out,
His faults so long and full?
The white rainbow adorned with clouds,
Why does it appear in this hall?
Where did he obtain the elixir,
Yet could not keep it secure?
The patterns of heaven crisscross,
When the yang spirit departs, death follows.
Why did the great bird cry out,
How did it lose its body?
Píng Hào brings the rain,
How does he stir it?
With a body joined at the ribs,
How does the deer bear it?
The turtle carries mountains and dances,
How are they stabilized?
Leaving the boat to travel on land,
How was it moved?
When Áo was at the door,
What did he seek from his sister-in-law?
Why did Shào Kāng set the hounds,
And cause his head to fall?
Nǚ Qí sewed his robes,
And shared his dwelling.
How was her head mistaken and severed,
And she met peril through intimacy?
Tāng planned to change his troops,
How did he strengthen them?
Overturning boats at Zhēn Xún,
By what means did he conquer?
Jié attacked Méng Shān,
What did he gain?
How did Mò Xǐ indulge,
And why did Tāng execute her?
Shun was troubled at home,
Yáo did not inform the Yáo family,
How did the two maidens become his wives?
The sprout was there at the start,
How could it be foreseen?
The jade tower of ten tiers,
Who planned it to such heights?
He ascended and became emperor,
By whose way was he exalted?
Nǚ Wā had her form,
Who crafted and shaped her?
Shun was kind to his brother,
Yet in the end, he was harmed.
How could he indulge a beastly nature,
And his own body not meet ruin?
Wú obtained an ancient legacy,
And settled at Nán Yuè.
Who expected that from this,
Two men would emerge?
Adorned with cranes and jade,
They feasted the Lord on High.
How did they inherit the plot against Jié of Xià,
Only to end in destruction?
The Lord descended to observe,
And below met Yī Zhì.
Why was he exiled to Tiáo and punished,
And the people greatly pleased?
Jiǎn Dí was in the tower, how did Kù find her fitting?
The dark bird brought the gift, why did the maiden rejoice?
Gāi upheld Jì's virtue,
His father praised him.
Why did he end in trouble with Yǒu Hù,
Tending oxen and sheep?
With shield and dance in time,
How did he win their hearts?
With smooth chest and fair skin,
How did he grow so stout?
The herdsman of Yǒu Hù,
How did they meet?
Struck in bed, he fled first,
From where did his fate come?
Héng upheld Jì's virtue,
Why go to manage ranks and rewards,
And not just return?
Hūn Wēi followed the path,
And Yǒu Dí knew no peace.
Why did flocks of birds gather on thorns,
And the son bear the blame wantonly?
The deluded brothers both lusted,
Endangering their elder.
How through deceit and change,
Did their descendants flourish long?
Chéng Tāng journeyed east,
Reaching Yǒu Shēn.
Why did he seek that humble servant,
And gain a lucky consort?
From the tree by the water's edge,
He obtained that little one.
Why did they despise him,
And send him as attendant to the woman of Yǒu Shēn?
Tāng emerged from Chóng Quán,
What crime had he committed?
Unable to bear his heart's urge, he attacked the emperor,
But who incited him?
They met at dawn to vie in alliance,
How did they keep our appointed time?
Grey birds flocking in flight,
Who gathered them?
They struck at Zhòu's person,
Yet Shū Dàn did not approve.
Why did he personally plan and launch the attack,
Yet sigh over Zhōu's mandate?
When heaven gave the Xià the world,
On what basis was its rule set?
It turned to success, then fell,
What was its crime?
Vying to send forth weapons of war,
How were they mobilized?
Driving together to strike the wings,
How were they commanded?
Zhāo Hòu embarked on a journey,
Reaching the southern lands.
What gain did he seek,
Encountering that white pheasant?
Mù Wáng was skilled in driving,
Why did he roam all around?
Circling and governing the world,
What was he searching for?
The eerie man flaunted his wares,
What was he crying in the market?
Who did Zhōu Yōu execute,
How did he obtain Bāo Sì?
Heaven's mandate is fickle,
What does it punish, what does it bless?
Qí Huán convened nine assemblies,
Yet in the end, he was killed.
In that person of King Zhòu,
Who caused the chaos and delusion?
Why did he detest loyal advisors,
And employ slanderers and flatterers?
What crime had Bǐ Gān committed,
That he was suppressed and sunk?
Léi Kāi assented and obeyed,
And was rewarded with fiefs?
Why do sages of one virtue, end in different ways?
Méi Bó was made into mincemeat,
Jī Zǐ feigned madness.
Jì was the firstborn son,
Why did the Lord on High treat him harshly?
Cast on the ice,
How did the birds warm him?
Why, with bow in hand and arrows ready,
Did he excel in leading troops?
Having alarmed the Lord so fiercely,
Why was he blessed with long life?
Bó Chāng led in decline,
Wielding the whip as a shepherd.
Why did he order the Qí shrine replaced,
And mandate the land of Yīn?
Moving treasures to Qí,
How could they rely on it?
Yīn had a bewitching woman,
What was there to criticize?
Receiving this gift of mincemeat,
Xī Bó appealed above.
Why did he personally bring heaven's punishment,
And Yīn's fate become unsalvageable?
Shī Wàng was in the market,
How did Chāng recognize him?
Wielding his knife and raising his voice,
Why did the lord rejoice?
Wǔ Fā killed the Yīn ruler,
Why was he troubled?
Carrying the corpse, he gathered for battle,
Why was he in such haste?
In Bó Lín, he hanged himself,
What was the reason?
How did it move heaven and shake the earth,
And whom did it frighten?
When heaven bestows the mandate,
What caution does it advise?
Receiving the rites to rule the world,
Why is it then replaced by another?
First, Tāng had minister Zhì,
later he served as assistant.
Why did he end up serving Tāng,
and was honored with temple sacrifices?
The meritorious Hé Lǚ dreamed of his birth,
but was orphaned and scattered young.
How did he grow fierce and martial,
able to spread his awe?
Péng Kēng cooked pheasant soup,
why did the Emperor enjoy it?
He received long life in abundance,
why did it last so long?
In the central plain, all herded,
why was the ruler angry?
The bee and ant, tiny creatures,
how were their forces so strong?
The maiden picking ferns was startled,
why did the deer protect her?
North to the winding river,
why was Cuì so joyful?
The elder brother had a fierce dog,
what did the younger desire?
He exchanged it for a hundred carriages,
and ended up without rank.
At dusk, thunder and lightning,
why worry about returning?
His majesty not upheld,
what could he ask of the Emperor?
Hiding in caves and dwelling,
what more could he say?
Jīng's merit in raising armies,
how could it last long?
Realizing faults and changing,
what more have I to say?
Wú Guāng contended for the state,
long did he defeat us.
Why, passing through villages and hills,
did Zǐ Wén emerge?
I told Dǔ Áo it would not last.
Why testing the sovereign and self-promoting,
made his loyal name more evident?
4.1 Lamenting My Oath
I lament my oath to express grief,
venting passion to pour out my feelings.
What I speak is from loyalty,
pointing to the blue sky as witness.
I bid the Five Emperors to judge fairly,
and summon the Six Spirits to testify.
Let mountains and rivers serve in court,
command Gāo Yáo to hear the case.
I exhaust loyalty to serve my lord,
yet am estranged like a wart.
Forgetting flattery, I turn from the crowd,
awaiting an enlightened lord to know me.
Words and deeds can be traced,
emotion and appearance unchanged.
So none knows a minister like his lord,
thus proof is not far.
My principle: lord first, self last,
yet the multitude hates me.
Devoted solely to my lord, no other,
again, the masses enmity me.
Single-minded and unwavering,
yet I cannot be preserved.
Eager to serve my lord, no other,
this is the way to invite disaster.
I think none is as loyal to the lord as I,
forgetting my lowly poverty.
Serving my lord without duplicity,
I'm lost, unaware of the path to favor.
Why is loyalty punished as crime?
This is not what my heart knew.
My conduct, unorthodox, leads to downfall,
and the masses mock me.
Frequently blamed and slandered,
I cannot explain it away.
Feelings suppressed, unexpressed,
obscured, with no chance to clarify.
My heart depressed, I falter,
none perceive my inner feelings.
Though many words can't be tied and sent,
I wish to state my will but find no way.
Retiring in silence, none know me,
advancing with cries, none hear me.
Repeatedly faltering, troubled and confused,
inwardly dismayed and distressed.
Once I dreamed of climbing to heaven,
my soul halfway, with no ferry.
I had the fierce god divine it,
saying: "You aim high but lack support."
Finally endangered, alone and estranged,
he said: "The lord can be longed for, not relied on."
For many mouths can melt metal,
from the start, thus, you met peril.
Burned by hot soup, one blows on cold,
why not change this resolve?
Wishing to discard the ladder and climb heaven,
you still have the old manner.
The crowd, terrified, loses heart,
how can they be companions?
Same goal but different paths,
how can they be allies?
Jìn's Shēn Shēng, a filial son,
his father believed slander, not loving him.
Stubbornly straightforward, unyielding,
Gǔn's achievements went unfulfilled.
I heard loyalty creates enmity,
casually thought it an exaggeration.
After nine broken arms, one becomes a doctor,
now I know it's true.
With darting arrows set above,
and nets spread below,
traps laid to amuse the lord,
I wish to retreat but have no place.
Wanting to linger and seek stay,
I fear more trouble and blame.
Wanting to fly high and afar,
the lord might ask, "Where are you going?"
Wanting to rush wildly off course,
my firm will cannot bear it.
Back and chest split, pain intertwines,
heart knotted and twisted in anguish.
I pound magnolia, strengthen huì,
grind shēn jiāo for grain.
Sow jiāng lí and grow chrysanthemums,
hoping to make fragrant spring food.
Fear my true feelings go uncredited,
so I reiterate to clarify myself.
Holding these virtues in seclusion,
I wish to reflect deeply and withdraw.
4.2 Crossing the River
From youth, I loved rare attire,
now old, it hasn't faded.
Wearing a long sword, dangling,
a cloud-piercing hat, towering.
Adorned with bright moon, girded with precious jade.
The world muddled, none know me,
I'll gallop high, unheeding.
Driving blue dragons, white serpents as team,
I roam with Chóng Huá in jade gardens.
Ascend Kūnlún, eat jade blooms,
with heaven and earth share longevity,
with sun and moon share radiance.
I mourn the southern tribes know me not,
at dawn, I cross Jiāng and Xiāng.
On È Zhǔ, I glance back,
sighing at autumn-winter's tail winds.
Walk my horse by hill shores,
park my carriage at Fāng Lín.
Boarding a boat, I sail up Yuán,
oars raised high, striking waves.
The boat drifts, not advancing,
stalled in swirling waters.
At dawn, set off from Wǎng Zhǔ,
by dusk, rest in Chén Yáng.
If my heart is upright,
though remote, what harm?
Entering Xù Pǔ, I wander,
lost, unaware where I go.
Deep woods, dark and dim,
where monkeys dwell.
Mountains steep, blocking sun,
below, shadowy and rainy.
Snowflakes boundless, thick,
clouds dense, touching eaves.
I mourn my joyless life,
alone in mountain seclusion.
I cannot change heart to follow customs,
thus destined for sorrow and hardship.
Jiē Yú shaved his head,
Sāng Hù walked naked.
Loyalty isn't always employed,
virtue isn't always used.
Wǔ Zǐ met disaster,
Bǐ Gān was minced.
All past eras were thus,
why blame today's people?
I'll hold to the path, unwavering,
destined for repeated darkness lifelong!
Epilogue:
Luan birds and phoenixes drift farther daily.
Sparrows and crows nest in halls and altars.
Lù shēn and xīn yí die in thickets.
Foul scents are used, fragrance can't approach.
Yin and yang swap places, times amiss.
Holding faith, yet dismayed,
Swiftly, I shall go forth!
4.3 Lament for Yǐng
Heaven's mandate is inconstant, alas,
Why terrify the people with calamities?
Families are torn apart and scattered,
In mid-spring we flee toward the east.
Leaving our homeland for distant lands,
We wander along Jiāng and Xià rivers.
Passing the capital gate with heavy heart,
On a jiǎ-day at dawn I set out.
Departing from Yǐngdū, leaving my home,
Bewildered, where is our journey's end?
Oars raised together, we drift slowly,
Grieving I'll never see my lord again.
Gazing at tall catalpas, I sigh deeply,
Tears streaming down like falling sleet.
Passing Xiàshǒu, floating westward,
Looking back, the dragon gate disappears.
My heart aches with lingering sorrow,
Not knowing where my steps may fall.
Following winds and waves downstream,
Adrift, I become a wandering stranger.
Riding Yánghóu's swelling waters,
Soaring like a bird, where to rest?
My heart is tangled and cannot loosen,
Thoughts knotted and cannot be freed.
Guiding my boat to float downstream,
Above is Dòngtíng, below the great river.
Leaving our ancestral dwelling place,
Now drifting freely toward the east.
My soul longs to return,
Not for a moment do I forget going back.
Turning from Xiàpǔ, thinking westward,
Sad the old capital grows more distant.
Climbing high ground to gaze afar,
Hoping to ease my anxious heart.
Mourning the peaceful land,
Lamenting Jiāngjiè's ancient customs.
Where shall I reach at Língyáng?
Vast southern crossing, where shall I go?
Never imagining palaces becoming mounds,
How could Yǐng's eastern gates grow wild?
My heart has long been joyless,
Worry and sorrow follow one another.
Thinking of Yǐng's road so distant,
Jiāng and Xià rivers cannot be crossed.
Time passes like an unbelievable dream,
Nine years now without returning.
Gloomy and depressed, no outlet,
Stumbling in distress, filled with grief!
Outwardly charming to please others,
Truly weak and unreliable.
Loyal and sincere, I wish to serve,
But envy spreads to block my way.
Yáo and Shùn's noble conduct,
Soared high and reached the heavens.
Slanderers' jealousy,
Falsely accused them of lacking compassion.
Disliking profound virtue's beauty,
Fond of hypocritical fervor.
Petty men crowd forward daily,
While the virtuous drift ever farther.
Finale:
Let me gaze in all directions,
Hoping to return once more—but when?
Birds fly back to their old nests,
Foxes die facing their native hills.
Truly, exiled though no crime of mine,
How could I forget, day or night?
4.4 Drawing forth My Thoughts
My heart, depressed with anxious thoughts,
Alone I sigh, increasingly grieved.
Brooding endlessly without relief,
How the night stretches on and on.
Saddened by the autumn wind's turmoil,
Why does the pole star sway so wildly?
Often thinking how my lord rages often,
Painting my anxious, troubled heart.
I'd rise and rush away impulsively,
But seeing people's woes, I restrain myself.
Gathering my feelings to compose these words,
I offer them to my fair lord.
Long ago you pledged your word to me,
Saying dusk would be our meeting time.
But you turned back midway,
Going another way with different intent.
You flaunt your beauty before me,
Display your elegance to my eyes.
Breaking your word when speaking with me,
Why seek reasons to be angry with me?
I'd seize a chance to explain myself,
But my heart trembles, I dare not;
Sadly hesitant, yet hoping to approach,
My heart aches, fearful and disturbed.
Listing my feelings in these words,
My lord feigns deafness, will not hear.
Sincere men naturally lack flattery,
So others take me for a trouble-maker.
What I stated first was clear and plain,
Could you have forgotten it by now?
Why speak so bluntly, like bitter medicine?
Hoping my lord's virtue may be perfected.
I hoped you'd emulate the Three Kings and Five Lords,
Taking Péngxián as your model.
No goal is beyond reach,
So your fame spreads far, enduring.
Virtue cannot come from outside,
Reputation cannot be built on emptiness.
Who can receive without giving?
Who can harvest without planting?
Short Song:
Pouring out grief to my fair lord,
Day and night, no one to judge fairly.
He flaunts his beauty before me,
Proudly ignoring all my words.
Chorus:
A bird from southern lands,
Alights north of the Hàn River.
Lovely and beautiful,
Alone in this strange country.
Solitary, without companions,
No good matchmaker at my side.
The road is long, memory fades daily,
I wish to plead but cannot.
Gazing toward Northern Mountain, tears flow,
Facing flowing water, deep sighs!
Looking at midsummer's short nights,
Why does darkness to dawn feel like a year?
Thinking of Yǐng's road so distant,
My soul travels there nine times each night.
Not knowing the road's twists and turns,
I guide south by moon and stars.
I wish to go directly but cannot,
My soul scurries, learning the way.
How faithful and true my soul is,
Others' hearts differ from mine!
My matchmaker unskilled, no message gets through,
None know my steadfast resolve.
Finale:
Long shoals, rushing currents, upstream I go.
Wildly gazing southward, to comfort my heart.
Jagged, towering rocks block my wish.
Veering from course, advancing slowly.
Hesitating, lingering, I lodge at Běigū.
Troubled, confused, truly rushing onward.
Sighing sadly, tormenting my spirit, my soul longs afar.
The road is far, the place remote, no messenger goes.
Thinking aloud, I make this song, to rescue myself.
My anxious heart finds no relief, to whom can I speak?
4.5 Embracing the Sand
Warm, flowing midsummer,
Plants and trees grow lush.
My heart grieves with endless sorrow,
Hurrying southward I go.
Looking around, all dim and silent,
Profoundly still and hushed.
Depressed, knotted with pain,
Suffering hardship, long distressed.
Examining my feelings, testing my resolve,
Wronged and constrained, I restrain myself.
They'd carve square into round,
But constant standards remain unchanged.
Changing one's original course,
Is despised by noble men.
Clear designs, marked with ink-lines,
Former plans not altered.
Sincere within, upright in substance,
Praised by great men.
If skillful Chuí didn't carve,
Who'd discern straight from crooked?
Dark patterns in shadows,
The blind say they show no light;
Lílóu squinting slightly,
The blind say he cannot see.
Turning white into black,
Upside down becomes bottom.
The phoenix confined in a cage,
While chickens and ducks dance freely.
Jade and stone mixed together,
Measured alike by one standard.
The faction's narrow-mindedness,
Cannot know my inner worth.
Bearing heavy loads, filled to capacity,
Stuck, unable to move forward.
Carrying gems, holding jades,
Poor, not knowing how to display them.
Village dogs barking in packs,
Bark at what seems strange.
Slandering wisdom, suspecting excellence,
Common behavior of mediocrity.
My substance and art are unadorned within,
The crowd knows not the extraordinary brilliance I possess.
Timber and simplicity lie in heaps,
None know what I have within.
I accumulate benevolence and righteousness,
Cautious and sincere to enrich myself.
Chóng Huá cannot be encountered,
Who knows my composure!
Since ancient times, some never meet,
How can we know the reason?
Tāng and Yǔ are long distant,
Far and beyond emulation.
I restrain resentment and curb anger,
Suppress my heart to strengthen myself.
Though suffering distress, I do not change,
Hoping my will has a model.
I advance northward to lodge,
As the day darkens toward dusk.
To ease sorrow and amuse grief,
Is bounded by the great end.
Epilogue:
Vast are Yuán and Xiāng,
Flowing separately and swiftly.
The long road is dark and obscured,
The way far and remote.
Holding substance and embracing emotion,
Alone I have no match.
Since Bólè is gone,
How can a steed be judged?
All people's lives,
Each have their place.
With settled heart and broad will,
What have I to fear?
Profound wounds and endless grief,
Eternal sighs I heave.
The world is murky, none know me,
Human hearts cannot be spoken to.
Knowing death cannot be avoided,
I wish not to cling to life.
Clearly I tell the noble man,
I will take him as my model.
4.6 Longing for the Fair One
Longing for the fair one,
I wipe my tears and gaze afar.
No matchmaker, the road is blocked,
Words cannot be tied and sent.
The distress of repeated loyalty,
Stuck and unable to express.
Daily I wish to pour out my heart,
But my will is stifled and unfulfilled.
I wish to entrust words to the floating clouds,
But meeting Fēng Lóng, they do not carry them.
I would send word by returning birds,
But they roost high and are hard to reach.
Gāo Xīn's divine abundance,
Met the dark bird to deliver gifts.
I wish to change and follow custom,
But ashamed to alter my start and bend my will.
Alone for years in suffering,
My resentful heart remains unchanged.
Rather bear sorrow to old age,
How can change be made!
Knowing the former path did not succeed,
I have not changed this course.
Though the cart overturned and horses fell,
I still cherish this different road.
Harnessing steeds to drive again,
Zào Fǔ would steer for me.
Moving slowly without haste,
Biding time with borrowed days.
Pointing to Bō Zhǒng's western slope,
I set dusk as the time.
As spring opens and the year begins,
The white sun rises leisurely.
I will free my heart and be joyful,
Following Jiāng and Xià to ease sorrow.
Gathering fragrant chǎi in thick woods,
Plucking perennial weeds on long isles.
Regretting I missed the ancients,
With whom to enjoy these fragrant plants?
I untie knotweed and mixed greens,
Preparing them as paired adornments.
Adornments tangled in profusion,
Then wither and fall apart.
I linger to amuse my sorrow,
Observing southerners' changing ways.
Secret joy within my heart,
Releasing my pent-up feelings without waiting.
Fragrance and moisture blend,
Yet fragrance emerges from within.
Rich and abundant, spreading far,
Full inside and radiating outward.
True feelings and substance can be preserved,
Though dwelling obscure, my fame spreads.
I'd have Bì Lì as envoy,
But fear to climb trees.
I'd ask lotus to be matchmaker,
But fear to wet my feet wading.
I dislike climbing high,
Nor can I descend low.
My form is naturally unaccustomed,
So I hesitate and doubt.
Fully pursuing former plans,
I have not changed this course.
Fate places me in darkness, I shall weary,
But wish to act before the sun sets.
Alone, solitary, I journey south,
Thinking of Péng Xián's example.
4.7 Lamenting Past Days
Lamenting past days when trusted,
I received commands to illuminate poetry.
Continuing ancestral deeds to enlighten below,
Clarifying doubts in laws and measures.
The state grew rich and laws established,
Entrusted to loyal ministers, the king amused daily.
Secret matters held in heart,
Even errors went unpunished.
Pure and earnest, not leaking secrets,
I met slanderers who envied me.
The king, angered, awaited his minister,
Not clarifying truth from falsehood.
Obscuring the king's wisdom,
They deceived with emptiness and confusion.
Without verification or checking facts,
They banished me far without reflection.
Believing slander's murkiness,
In high dudgeon, he punished me.
Why is a loyal minister guiltless,
Yet slandered and blamed?
Ashamed of light and shadow's honesty,
I hide in obscurity, prepared.
Facing Yuán and Xiāng's dark depths,
I resolve to endure and sink.
Finally perishing, name cut off,
Regretting the blinded king's ignorance.
The king, without measure, unseeing,
Makes fragrant grass haunt marshy shadows.
Where to express feelings and draw forth truth?
Calm in death, I will not cling to life.
Alone, blocked and hidden,
Loyal ministers have no way.
Hearing Bǎi Lǐ was a captive,
Yī Yǐn cooked in the kitchen.
Lǚ Wàng butchered in Zhāo Gē,
Nìng Qì sang while feeding oxen.
Without meeting Tāng, Wǔ, Huán, or Mù,
Who in the world would know them?
Wú believed slander without tasting truth,
Zǐ Xū died, then came regret.
Jiè Zǐ loyal and stood dried up,
Wén Lord awoke and sought him.
Sealing Jiè Mountain as forbidden ground,
Repaying great virtue leisurely.
Thinking of an old friend close at hand,
In plain white, he wept for him.
Some die faithful and loyal,
Some deceitful yet unsuspected.
Without examination or checking facts,
Heeding slanderers' empty words.
Fragrance and moisture blend,
Who can distinguish them at dawn?
Why do fragrant plants die young?
Frost descends as warning.
Indeed, hearing unclear and blocked,
Letting slanderers daily prosper.
Since ancient times, envying the worthy,
Saying orchids should not be worn.
Jealous of beauty's fragrance,
Mó Mǔ preens herself.
Even with Xī Shī's fair looks,
Slander and envy intrude to replace.
Wishing to state my case and clear my actions,
I incurred blame unexpectedly.
Truth and injustice daily clearer,
Like constellations arrayed.
Riding a steed to gallop,
Without reins, self-reliant;
Riding a raft downstream,
Without oars, self-prepared.
Abandoning laws for whims,
Is no different from this.
Rather die suddenly and vanish,
Fearing disaster may recur.
Not finishing words, I go to the abyss,
Regretting the blinded king's ignorance.
4.8 Ode to the Orange Tree
Splendid tree of earth and heaven,
Orange, you adapt here.
Receiving fate unchanging,
Born in the southern land.
Deep-rooted, hard to move,
More steadfast in will.
With closed heart and self-caution, I shall not repeatedly err.
Holding virtue without selfishness, I match heaven and earth.
I wish to wither with the seasons, and befriend the enduring.
Pure and untainted, steadfast with principles.
Though young in years, fit to be a teacher.
Conduct rivaling Bó Yí, I set him as my model.
4.9 Lamenting the Whirlwind
I lament the whirlwind shaking the orchids,
My heart knotted with grievance, wounded within.
Things, though subtle, can lose their nature,
Sounds, though faint, can lead the chorus.
Why do I dwell on Péng Xián's thoughts,
And his steadfast resolve, never forgotten!
Can countless changes in emotion be concealed?
What hypocrisy can long endure!
Birds and beasts cry to call their flocks,
Weeds cluster together but lack fragrance.
Fish array their scales to stand out,
While jiāo dragons hide their patterns.
Thus thistles and shepherd's purse don't share a field,
Orchids and angelica bloom alone in seclusion.
Only the noble one remains eternally fair,
Through changing eras, self-bestowed.
My lofty aspirations reach afar,
Pitying the drifting clouds' wanderings.
Troubled by my subtle ambitions,
I secretly compose poems to clarify them.
Only the noble one holds unique thoughts,
Plucking dùn and pepper to dwell alone.
Repeatedly sighing with sobs,
Solitarily hidden, pondering deeply.
Tears streaming down, desolate and cold,
Thoughts keep me awake till dawn.
Through the long, endless night,
This sorrow lingers, refusing to depart.
Awake, I roam at ease,
Lingering in carefree self-reliance.
Grieved by deep sighs of compassion,
Breath choked, unstoppable.
Twisting my thoughts into a sash,
Weaving sorrows into a breastplate.
Breaking the ruò tree to block the light,
Following the whirlwind's course.
Visions exist yet remain unseen,
My heart boils like bubbling water.
Stroking my sash to calm my will,
I wander dazed and proceed.
Years slip away as if collapsing,
Time gradually approaches its end.
Fragrant herbs wither, joints separating,
Their scent fades, no longer clustered.
Pitying my unstoppable pensive heart,
Proving these words offer no solace.
Rather die and drift away,
Than endure this constant sorrow.
An orphan sighs and wipes tears,
An outcast leaves, never to return.
Who can ponder without hidden pain?
I emulate what I've heard of Péng Xián.
Climbing stony peaks to gaze afar,
The road stretches silently into obscurity.
Entering scenes with no echo or response,
Reflection and longing yield nothing.
Melancholy without joy,
Dwelling in grief, inextricable.
My heart restrained, unexpressed,
Breath tangled, self-bound.
Vast and boundless, without limits,
Wild and dim, without form.
Sounds, though faint, resonate,
Things, pure in essence, remain unattainable.
Distant and endless, immeasurable,
Ethereal and continuous, unyielding.
Quiet sorrow, constant grief,
Soaring into darkness, devoid of joy.
Riding great waves with the flowing wind,
I seek Péng Xián's abode.
Ascending steep cliffs of high peaks,
Perching atop the rainbow's arch.
Leaning on the azure to unleash the rainbow,
Suddenly, I touch the sky.
Sipping from the deep source of clear dew,
Gargling with crystallized frost, flake by flake.
Resting by the wind cave,
Suddenly I awaken, trembling with emotion.
Mounting Kūnlún to gaze upon the mist,
Peering from Mínshān at the clear river.
Dreading the roaring torrents,
Hearing the tumultuous waves.
Chaos without order,
Confusion without pattern.
Crushing waves, directionless,
Flowing bends, where do they cease?
Drifting up and down, tossing,
Wings fluttering left and right.
Surging front and back,
Following the rhythm of ebb and flow.
Observing the rising heat waves,
Watching the accumulation of mist and dew.
Grieving the fall of frost and snow,
Listening to the clash of tides.
Borrowing light and shadow to travel,
Wielding a crooked whip of yellow thorns.
Seeking where Jiè Zǐ dwelled,
Witnessing Bó Yí's exiled traces.
My heart deliberates, unwilling to leave,
Engraving my resolve, with nowhere to turn.
I say:
I regret the hopes of past days,
Mourn the anxiety of times to come.
Floating on Cháng Jiāng and Huái River into the sea,
Following Wǔ Zǐxū to find peace.
Gazing at the isles of the great river,
Lamenting Shēn Tú's noble traces.
Repeatedly advising the lord unheeded,
What good is bearing heavy stones?
My heart entangled, unresolved,
Thoughts knotted, unreleased.
I grieve at the world's oppressive strife,
Wishing to rise lightly and wander far.
My substance too meager, without means,
How to ride aloft and float above?
Encountering filth and corruption,
Alone in melancholy, whom to tell!
Restless through the night, sleepless,
My lonely soul reaches dawn.
Reflecting on heaven and earth's infinity,
I mourn life's endless toil.
The past I could not reach,
The future I shall not hear.
Pacing, leaning, lost in distant thoughts,
Distraught and bewildered, my heart astray.
My mind drifts in confusion,
My heart saddens, grief deepening.
My spirit wanders, not returning,
My body withered, left alone.
Introspecting to rectify my conduct,
Seeking the source of upright energy.
Serene in emptiness and stillness, content,
Tranquil in non-action, self-possessed.
Hearing of Chìsōngzǐ's pure dust,
I wish to follow his legacy.
Valuing the true man's virtuous rest,
Admiring the transcendents of old.
They transformed and vanished from sight,
Their fame enduring, ever-spreading.
Marveling at Fù Yuè's lodging in the stars,
Envying Hán Zhòng's unity with the Dào,
Their forms serene, fading afar,
Departing the crowd, escaping worldly ties.
Through breath's change, they soared high,
Suddenly like spirits dashing, ghostly strange.
At times glimpsed from afar,
Their essence bright, coming and going.
Beyond dust and turmoil, to blessed realms,
Never returning to their homeland.
Free from all fears, unafraid,
The world knows not where they've gone.
Fearing the seasons' relentless change,
The radiant sun blazes westward.
Light frost descends and sinks,
I mourn the fragrant herbs' early withering.
Lingering aimlessly, wandering free,
Passing years with no achievement.
Who can share these fading scents with me?
At dawn, I face the wind to express my feelings.
Gāo Yáng is remote and far,
Where shall I find my model?
I reiterate:
Spring and autumn swiftly pass, not lingering,
Why long remain in this old abode?
Xuān Yuán is beyond reach,
I'll follow Wáng Zǐ Qiáo for joy and play!
Feeding on six breaths, drinking night dew,
Rinsing with zhèng yáng, imbibing morning mist.
Preserving spirit's clarity,
Essence enters, coarse impurities depart.
Riding the south wind to wander,
To Nán Cháo I rest awhile.
Meeting the prince, I lodge with him,
Inquiring about the harmony of the one breath.
He says:
"The Dào can be received,
But not transmitted;
So small, it has no inside,
So vast, it has no bounds;
Let not your soul be confused,
And it will become natural;
Concentrate the vital force with deep spirituality,
Preserving it in the midnight hour;
Remain empty to receive it,
Do not act before it comes;
All things will thus be accomplished,
This is the gate of virtue.
Hearing of the supreme value, I set forth,
Swiftly I am about to journey.
Following the feathered men to Dānqiū,
I linger in the ancient land of immortality.
At dawn I wash my hair in Yánggǔ,
At dusk I dry myself under the nine suns.
I sip the fine liquid of the flying spring,
Cherishing the radiant blossoms of Wǎnyǎn.
My jade-like face glows with a ruddy complexion,
My essence, pure and unadulterated, begins to strengthen.
My substance melts away, becoming supple and graceful,
My spirit, subtle and profound, roams freely.
I admire the fiery virtue of the southern lands,
The beautiful cassia trees blooming in winter.
The mountains are desolate, without beasts,
The wilderness silent, without people.
Carrying my soul, I ascend on the rosy clouds,
Shrouded in floating mists, I soar upward.
I command the heavenly gatekeeper to open the gates,
He pushes open the Chānghé and gazes at me.
I summon Fēnglóng to lead the way,
Inquiring the abode of the Great Subtlety.
Gathering at the double brightness, I enter the emperor's palace,
Visiting Xúnshǐ to behold the pure capital.
At dawn I set off from Tàiyí,
By dusk I arrive at Yúwēilǘ.
Marshaling my ten thousand chariots,
They surge forward in majestic array.
Driving eight dragons, winding and graceful,
Bearing cloud banners, undulating and long.
Erecting the rainbow's colored streamers,
Blending five hues, dazzling and bright.
The main steeds, proud and dipping low,
The side horses, coiled and prancing high.
The riders press close in chaotic throngs,
In sprawling lines, they march abreast.
Gripping my reins and adjusting my whip,
I shall pass by Jùmáng.
Passing Tàihào and turning right,
With Fēilián ahead to clear the path.
The sun, bright but not yet fully lit,
I traverse heaven and earth directly.
The Wind Earl acts as my vanguard,
Clearing dust and haze, bringing coolness.
The phoenix spreads its wings to uphold the banners,
Meeting Rùshōu at the Western Emperor's court.
Seizing a comet to serve as my pennant,
Raising the Dipper's handle as my command flag.
In dazzling confusion, up and down,
Drifting through the swirling mists like flowing waves.
The time is dim and obscure,
I summon Xuánwǔ to rush and attend.
Appointing Wénchāng to oversee the march,
Selecting various deities to ride alongside.
The road stretches far and endless,
Slowly I rein in and soar high.
On the left, the Rain Master stands ready,
On the right, the Thunder God acts as guard.
Wishing to transcend the world and forget return,
My heart is carefree and unrestrained.
Within, joyful and self-admiring,
I find solace in amusement and self-delight.
Wandering freely through the azure clouds,
Suddenly I glance down at my old homeland.
My attendants grieve, my heart saddens,
The side horses look back and refuse to advance.
Thinking of old friends and imagining them,
I heave long sighs and wipe away tears.
Drifting at ease, yet soaring afar,
I suppress my will to calm myself.
Pointing to Yánshén, I charge straight ahead,
I shall go to Nányí.
Gazing at the wild and indistinct beyond,
I float freely in the boundless void.
Zhùróng warns and turns the carriage around,
Sending word for the simurgh to welcome Fúfēi.
Performing the "Xiánchí" and playing the "Chéngyún,"
The two maidens present the "Jiǔsháo" song.
Having the Xiāng River spirit play the se,
Commanding Hǎiruò and Féngyí to dance.
Dark dragons and elephant-like creatures emerge together,
Their forms coiling and winding.
The female rainbow, graceful and twisting,
The simurgh soars and flies aloft.
The music expands without end,
Then I depart, yet linger in hesitation.
Loosening the reins to gallop freely,
I reach the farthest shores at the cold gate.
Outpacing the swift wind at the clear source,
I follow Zhuānxū over layered ice.
Passing Xuánmíng by a winding path,
Riding the gaps between dimensions, I look back.
Summoning Qiánléi for an audience,
He paves the way for me on level ground.
Journeying through the four wilds,
Roaming across the six desolations.
Ascending to the arrayed gaps,
Descending to gaze into the great abyss.
Below, profound and without ground,
Above, vast and without sky.
Looking swiftly, I see nothing,
Listening intently, I hear nothing.
Transcending non-action to reach utmost clarity,
I become the neighbor of the Great Beginning.
After Qū Yuán was exiled, for three years he could not see the king again.
He exhausted his wisdom and loyalty,
Yet was obstructed by slander.
His heart troubled, his thoughts confused,
He did not know where to turn.
He went to see the Grand Diviner Zhèng Zhānyǐn and said:
"I have some doubts,
And wish to rely on you, sir, to resolve them."
Zhānyǐn then arranged the stalks and brushed the tortoise shell,
Saying: "What would you have me do for you?"
Qū Yuán said:
"Should I be sincere and earnest,
Simple and loyal?
Or pursue social comings and goings without end?
Should I cut down weeds
And labor in farming?
Or seek out great men
To achieve fame?
Should I speak truthfully without concealment,
Even at the risk of my life?
Or follow vulgar customs for wealth and honor,
To save my life?
Should I rise above and hold myself aloft
To preserve my integrity?
Or flatter and fawn,
Cringing and fawning,
To serve women?
Should I be honest and upright
To keep myself pure?
Or be slick and glib,
Like grease or soft leather,
To smooth the pillars?
Should I hold my head high like a thousand-mile steed?
Or float aimlessly like a duck in water,
Rising and falling with the waves,
To preserve my body?
Should I yoke myself with fine steeds?
Or follow in the tracks of nags?
Should I soar wing to wing with the yellow swan?
Or fight for food with chickens and ducks?
Which is auspicious, which is ominous?
What should I avoid, what should I follow?"
"The world is muddy and unclear,
Where cicada wings are heavy,
And a thousand jun are light;
The yellow bell is cast aside,
While earthen pots thunder;
Slanderers are exalted,
While worthy men remain unknown.
Alas, in silence,
Who knows my integrity and faithfulness!"
Zhānyǐn then set aside the stalks and declined, saying:
"A foot may sometimes fall short,
An inch may sometimes suffice;
Things have their deficiencies,
Wisdom has its uncertainties;
Calculation has its limits,
The divine has its obscurities.
Use your own heart,
Follow your own will,
The tortoise and stalks truly cannot know these matters."
After Qū Yuán was exiled, he wandered by the river pools,
Chanting as he walked along the marsh's edge,
His countenance haggard,
His appearance withered.
A fisherman saw him and asked:
"Are you not the Sānlǘ Dàfū?
What brings you to this state?"
Qū Yuán said:
"The whole world is muddy, only I am clear;
Everyone is drunk, only I am sober;
Therefore I am exiled."
The fisherman said:
"The sage is not rigidly attached to things,
But can move with the world.
If the world is muddy,
Why not stir up the mud and ride the waves?
If everyone is drunk,
Why not eat the dregs and drink the lees?
Why deep thoughts and lofty actions,
Bringing exile upon yourself?"
Qū Yuán said:
"I have heard it said,
'One who has just washed his hair must brush his cap;
one who has just bathed must shake out his clothes.'
How can one with a body so pure
endure the contamination of the world?
I would rather plunge into the Xiāng River's flow,
and be buried in the bellies of its fish.
How can one with such spotless purity
be sullied by the dust of the vulgar world?"
The fisherman smiled faintly,
and rowed away,
singing:
"When the Cānglàng's waters are clear,
I can wash my hat-strings;
when the Cānglàng's waters are muddy,
I can wash my feet."
He then departed, speaking no more.
How sorrowful is autumn's breath!
Desolate and dreary,
plants and trees wither and decay;
melancholy,
as if on a distant journey;
climbing hills and facing waters,
seeing travelers homeward bound;
vast and empty,
the sky high and air clear;
still and silent,
floods receded and waters clear;
grieving with added sighs,
as the slight chill strikes one;
disconsolate and forlorn,
leaving the old for the new;
disheartened,
a poor scholar out of office, his will unsettled;
lonely,
a traveler with no friends;
dispirited,
privately pitying myself.
Swallows fly gracefully, taking leave;
cicadas fall silent, without a sound.
Wild geese honk as they journey south;
pheasants chirp plaintively.
Alone, I stay awake till dawn,
lamenting the crickets' nightly marches.
Time slips by past its midpoint;
I linger in vain, achieving nothing!
Sorrowful, worried, destitute, alone in emptiness,
a beauty with a heart unconsoled.
Leaving home and family, I come as a distant guest;
wandering aimlessly, where shall I find rest?
Devotedly thinking of my lord, unchangeable;
my lord does not know me—what can I do!
Accumulating resentment and thoughts,
my heart troubled, forgetting food and drink.
I wish to see him once to express my intent,
but his heart differs from mine.
The chariot is harnessed, I set off to return;
unable to see him, my heart grieves.
Leaning on the crossbar, I heave long sighs;
tears flow down, wetting the yoke.
Unable to break off in indignation,
my mind confused and bewildered.
Privately pitying myself without end,
my heart pounds, loyal and upright.
Heaven divides the four seasons equally,
yet I secretly mourn this bleak autumn.
White dew has descended on all plants;
suddenly, the wú and qiū trees shed their leaves.
Leaving the bright brilliance of day,
I enter the long, endless night.
Departing from the fragrant prime of youth,
I wither and grieve in sorrow.
Autumn first warns with white dew,
winter follows with severe frost.
Gathering in the lushness of early summer,
then halting and sinking into hiding.
Leaves dull and colorless;
branches tangled and crosswise;
complexions fading and weary;
trunks gaunt and withered yellow;
the sparse treetops pitiable;
forms emaciated and bruised.
As they mingle and are about to fall,
I regret they've missed their time and are unappreciated.
Taking the reins and slowing the pace,
I wander aimlessly for a while.
The year hurries to its end;
I fear my life will not last long.
Mourning that I was born at the wrong time,
I encounter this age of turmoil.
Calm and leisurely, I stand alone;
crickets chirp in the western hall.
My heart alarmed and shaken,
how many are the sources of my worries!
Gazing at the bright moon, I sigh;
walking among the stars till dawn.
I secretly grieve for the huì flowers that once bloomed,
so luxuriant in the grand chamber.
Why did their abundant blossoms bear no fruit,
scattering in the wind and rain?
I thought you alone wore this huì,
yet it proved no different from common flowers.
Pitying that my unusual thoughts go unheeded,
I shall leave you and soar high.
My heart, compassionate and sorrowful,
wishes to see you once for clarity.
Though blameless, I face separation;
my heart knots with added grief.
How can I not yearn and think of you?
But your gate is ninefold deep.
Fierce dogs bark fiercely on my approach;
passes and bridges closed and impassable.
Heaven pours with autumn rains;
when will the earth ever dry!
Alone, I guard this marshy land,
gazing at floating clouds with eternal sighs.
How cunning is the fashion of the times,
turning from the ink-line and altering measures!
Rejecting fine steeds, they do not ride them;
urging on nags, they take to the road.
Is there no fine steed in this age?
Truly, none can handle them well.
Seeing the reins held by the wrong hands,
they bolt and flee far away.
Ducks and geese peck at grain and weeds,
while the phoenix soars ever higher.
A round peg in a square hole—
I knew it would not fit.
All birds have perches to rest on;
the phoenix alone roams with nowhere to alight.
I wish to hold a tally and remain silent,
but I have received your deep kindness.
Jiang Ziya gained honor at ninety;
truly, he had not met his match before.
Where shall the fine steed return?
Where shall the phoenix perch?
Changing ancient ways and customs, the world declines;
now those who judge look only at fatness.
Fine steeds hide and are unseen;
phoenixes fly high and do not descend.
Even birds and beasts know to cherish virtue;
why say that worthy men do not stay?
The steed does not rush forward to be tamed;
the phoenix does not greedily eat recklessly.
You reject and ignore me without discernment;
though I wish to be loyal, how can I achieve it?
I wish to be silent and sever all ties,
but secretly I dare not forget your initial kindness.
Alone in sorrow, it wounds the heart;
how endless is this pent-up gloom!
Frost and dew fall bleakly together;
my heart still hopes they may not succeed.
Sleet and snow mix and increase;
I hope for luck and wait,
adrift in vast wilderness, dying with weeds.
I wish to go directly to you,
but the road is blocked and impassable.
I want to follow the path and drive steadily,
yet I know not where to turn.
Thus, midway, I am confused;
I restrain myself and learn to chant.
By nature foolish, narrow, and shallow,
I am truly not adept at ease.
I secretly admire Shēn Bāoxū's fervent spirit,
but fear the times are not steadfast.
How cunning is the fashion of the times?
They discard compass and square, altering carvings.
Alone, upright and unyielding, I do not follow;
I wish to emulate the teachings of ancient sages.
To be illustrious in a corrupt world
is not what my heart delights in.
Rather than fame without righteousness,
I'd stay poor and uphold my virtue.
I eat not to fill myself through deceit;
I dress not to keep warm through compromise.
I secretly admire the poets' legacy;
I wish to entrust my will to simple fare.
Stubborn and unyielding without cause,
adrift in boundless wilderness.
I have no furs to ward off winter;
I fear sudden death before seeing spring.
In the deep night of late autumn,
my heart tangled and sorrowful.
The years stretch on, and I grow older;
thus disconsolate, I grieve alone.
The four seasons alternate to end the year;
yin and yang cannot keep pace together.
The pale sun wanes as it sets;
the bright moon wanes and diminishes.
The year hurries to its end;
age advances, and I grow slack.
My heart wavers with fleeting joy yet daily hopes,
But then I'm despondent with no expectations.
Within, pained and grieved in sorrow,
I heave long sighs, adding to my sobs.
Years drift by as days pass,
Aging in vast emptiness with no place to rest.
Affairs press on as I hope to advance,
Yet I linger hesitantly, stuck in indecision.
Why do the floating clouds run rampant,
Swiftly obscuring this bright moon!
My loyalty shines bright, wishing to be seen,
But overcast skies block its reach.
I long for the bright sun to manifest its course,
Yet dense clouds shroud it.
Secretly, I cannot bear it but wish to be loyal,
Yet some smear and tarnish me.
Yáo and Shùn's lofty deeds,
So profound they touched the heavens.
Why do the envious, with their treacherous schemes,
Slander them with false names of lacking kindness?
Even the sun and moon that illuminate,
Still have dim spots and flaws.
How much more the affairs of a state,
Entangled and complex in many ways.
Clad in a lotus robe, soft and gentle,
Yet too loose to be fastened.
Proud of beauty and boasting of might,
Betraying the loyalty of those around.
Disliking the virtuous and refined,
Favoring the ostentatious and loud.
The crowd jostles forward daily,
While the noble drift further away.
Farmers abandon their plows to idle,
Fearing the fields will grow wild.
Affairs drag on, filled with selfishness,
The world echoes blindly in dazzling show,
How confused are the slanders and praises!
Now I groom myself and peer in the mirror,
Hoping later to find refuge.
I wish to send a word by the shooting star,
But it flashes past, too swift to catch.
Ultimately blocked by these floating clouds,
The world below is dim and lightless.
Yáo and Shùn had those they appointed,
Thus they rested easy, content.
Truly, without enmity from the world,
Why should the heart feel this fear?
Riding fine steeds that glide smoothly,
What need for harsh whips in guidance?
Indeed, city walls are not enough to rely on,
Even with heavy armor, what good is it?
Wandering cautiously but without end,
Depressed and confused, bound by sorrow.
Life between heaven and earth is but a passing,
With no achievement and no effect.
I wish to sink into obscurity unseen,
Yet still hope to spread my name under heaven.
But drifting without encounter,
I'm merely foolish, tormenting myself.
Vast and boundless without limits,
Where can I soar and alight?
The state has fine steeds but doesn't ride them,
Why rush about seeking elsewhere?
Nìng Qì sang at the carriage's foot,
Duke Huán heard and knew his worth.
Without a Bólè skilled in judging,
Who now will praise them?
In vain, I shed tears and ponder,
Only with intent focus can one grasp it.
Sincerely, purely, I wish to be loyal,
But envy spreads and obstructs it.
I beg to take my unworthy body and depart,
To set my wanderlust free in the clouds.
Riding the swirling essence of vital breath,
Chasing the profound gods in their majesty.
Harnessed to white rainbows, gliding smoothly,
Passing through throngs of spirits in abundance.
On the left, the Vermilion Bird flutters,
On the right, the Azure Dragon strides.
Followed by the thunder god's rumble,
And met by the wind god's procession.
Ahead, light carriages clatter,
Behind, heavy wagons follow in train.
Banners of cloud streamers undulating,
Escorted by clustered riders in grandeur.
My resolve, steadfast and unchangeable,
I hope to push forward for the good.
Relying on the great virtue of august heaven,
May it extend to you, lord, free from harm.
I was pure and honest from youth,
Devoted to righteousness, never fading.
Upholding this abundant virtue,
Yet dragged by customs into decay.
The ruler did not examine this virtue,
So I long suffered distress and sorrow.
God told Wū Yáng:
"There is a man below; I wish to aid him.
His soul has scattered; divine and return it!"
Wū Yáng replied:
